strengths: Addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text generation: subject overlap, repeated text stimuli, and overlapping temporal windows can obscure what a model generalizes to.

Examines five splitting strategies across EEG and fMRI datasets, evaluates two established models, and reports leakage statistics across four seeds. The reported results demonstrate substantial sensitivity to evaluation protocol.
Jointly withholding subjects and stimuli is appropriate for the stated goal of decoding unseen text from unseen subjects. The manuscript also acknowledges the resulting data-discarding tradeoff.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claims are insufficiently supported. In Section 4.4, decreasing reconstruction validation loss and increasing decoding scores with longer training are interpreted as encoder degradation and decoder memorization, although these trends also occur during ordinary learning. The EEG curves do not establish the claimed encoder effect. Shuffled-signal, no-signal, and text-only controls are needed to determine whether predictions actually depend on brain information.

The comparisons do not isolate the effects of leakage. Table 2 changes encoder initialization, learning rate, and training duration simultaneously; a randomly initialized encoder still receives informative signals. The proposed split also changes subject and stimulus distributions and discards an unreported quantity of data. Matched training budgets, retained sample counts, and controlled comparisons are needed before attributing performance differences specifically to contamination.

The paper conflates distinct generalization targets. Training and testing on different recordings from the same subject can legitimately evaluate personalized decoding of unseen text. Joint subject-and-stimulus holdout evaluates a stricter deployment setting, but this does not establish that every within-subject evaluation is contaminated or that its encoder is corrupted. Criticism of prior protocols should be tied to their stated generalization claims.

The supplied splitting pseudocode does not preserve its central guarantee as written. Algorithm 1, line 15, checks subject membership when restoring edges but does not exclude text assigned to validation or test, permitting stimulus overlap to reappear. Algorithm 2, line 33, has the corresponding omission for subject membership. The initialization loops also conflict with the graph dimensions and prose description. These issues require corrected pseudocode and verification of the actual experimental partitions.

The quantitative reporting needs correction. Equation 7 measures intersections of individual signal samples, whereas the surrounding definition concerns shared subject identity; distinct recordings from shared subjects need not intersect. Its denominator also requires handling subjects absent from training. Additionally, Table 3 reports ROUGE-1 F = 84.64 with P = 63.16 and R = 71.50 for UniCoRN under 80+1e-4+(c), which is incompatible with standard, consistently aggregated F-scores.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the claimed benchmark release. The manuscript provides no benchmark/code link or exact split manifests, retained subject/story/sample counts, or sufficiently explicit decoding and checkpoint-selection procedures. Generation results lack reported variability across splits or training runs; the four-seed analysis concerns leakage statistics. Together with the unsupported causal interpretations and algorithm inconsistencies, these concerns prevent a sound Findings recommendation. Corrected specifications and targeted experimental reruns make next-cycle resubmission appropriate.
